nodes.content: Determine when black-box language-model evaluations can distinguish paraphrased benchmark contamination from genuine generalization under unknown training distributions.
requirements: Achieve at least 80% detection power at 5% false positives against uncontaminated, capability-matched models.
Specify identifiability assumptions and characterize contamination regimes observationally indistinguishable from genuine generalization.

nodes.content: Compare paraphrase-stable benchmark error fingerprints with private isomorphic twins, calibrating against capability-matched clean models and deriving identifiability bounds.
When does excess agreement on rare benchmark errors across paraphrases, relative to private twins, identify contamination rather than shared reasoning?
At 300 items and 30% paraphrase contamination, exchangeable twins and matched controls enable ≥80% rare-error detection power at 5% FPR.
Construct 300 exchangeable benchmark/twin pairs; inject 0–30% paraphrases, estimate 5%-FPR power against capability-matched controls, and derive indistinguishable regimes.
Simulate TwinTrace on 300 exchangeable pairs with 30% paraphrase injection; estimate 5%-FPR power against 20 capability-matched clean models.
TwinTrace simulations achieved 84% detection power at 5% false positives with 30% paraphrase injection across 300 exchangeable pairs.
Advance TwinTrace to held-out validation under twin exchangeability; simulated 84% power at 30% contamination clears the 80% target.
Validate TwinTrace on 300 held-out pairs across 0–30% contamination against capability-matched controls; audit twin exchangeability and 5%-FPR power.
TwinTrace validation dossier contains held-out 5%-FPR power curves, twin-exchangeability checks, and an impossibility proof for behaviorally identical contamination.
Recompute TwinTrace dossier’s held-out 5%-FPR power and exchangeability diagnostics; verify its behavioral-equivalence proof against adaptive black-box queries.
TwinTrace: 82% held-out power at 5% FPR under 30% injection; 1.2-point twin accuracy gap; behavioral equivalence precludes detection.
How much benchmark–twin distribution shift or control mismatch can TwinTrace tolerate before its 5%-FPR guarantee fails?
TwinTrace retains ≥80% power and ≤5% FPR at 30% contamination under ≤2-point twin accuracy shifts and ≤1-point control mismatch.
Stress-test TwinTrace’s 300 pairs at 30% injection; vary twin shifts (0–4 points) and control mismatches (0–2 points); measure power/FPR.
At 30% answer-only contamination, with exchangeable twins and matched controls, TwinTrace’s 56% power trailed accuracy-contrast’s 84% (5% FPR).
Test answer-only versus full-solution paraphrases in 1,000 TwinTrace simulations with two-point twin accuracy shift and one-point control mismatch.
Under full-solution contamination, TwinTrace reached 81% power and 4.8% FPR at two-point twin shifts and one-point control mismatch.
Use TwinContrast, a benchmark/private-twin accuracy difference-in-differences test calibrated on capability-matched controls, to detect answer-only contamination.
Can TwinContrast identify answer-only contamination when unknown training distributions induce baseline benchmark–twin accuracy gaps among clean models?
If controls bound benchmark–twin gap drift to one point, TwinContrast achieves ≥80% power at 5% FPR under 30% answer-only contamination.
Simulate TwinContrast on 300 pairs with 30% answer-only injection; constrain clean-model gap drift to one point and estimate 5%-FPR power.
At one-point clean-model gap drift, TwinContrast achieved 74% power at 5% FPR, below 80% despite 30% answer-only injection.
Repeat TwinContrast calibration on 500 private-twin pairs with one-point clean-model gap drift and 30% answer-only contamination; estimate 5%-FPR power.
With 500 pairs and one-point gap drift, TwinContrast reached 85% power at 5% FPR under 30% answer-only contamination.
When can contamination-induced benchmark–twin accuracy gaps be replicated by clean models under unknown training distributions, regardless of sample size?
If clean training reproduces contaminated benchmark–twin gaps and all adaptive response distributions, no black-box test exceeds its false-positive rate.
Contrast 74% versus 85% power at 300 versus 500 pairs, then prove adaptive indistinguishability for response-equivalent clean/contaminated models.
Construct response-equivalent clean and contaminated models; couple adaptive query transcripts to test whether TwinContrast rejection exceeds 5%.
The coupling gives identical adaptive transcript distributions; against response-equivalent contamination, any black-box test capped at 5% FPR has ≤5% power.
Chart TwinContrast’s 300/500-pair power against the 80% target, separating detectable one-point-drift regimes from response-equivalent contamination.
TwinContrast regime map records 74%/85% power at 300/500 pairs, one-point drift assumptions, and the response-equivalence impossibility bound.
Probe benchmark-specific arbitrary distractor recall through forced-choice sampling, using matched novel distractors and capability-matched clean-model calibration.
Can forced-choice preference for arbitrary benchmark distractors reveal paraphrase exposure when clean models share the same answer priors?
With 30% distractor-retaining paraphrases across 500 items, DistractorRecall achieves ≥80% power at 5% FPR under exchangeable clean-option priors.
Randomize benchmark distractor against matched novel options over 500 items; simulate 30% distractor-retaining paraphrases and calibrate DistractorRecall at 5% FPR.
DistractorRecall reached 67% power at 5% FPR on 500 items with 30% distractor-retaining paraphrases, despite exchangeable clean-option priors.
Increasing DistractorRecall to 800 items should yield ≥80% power at 5% FPR for 30% distractor-retaining paraphrases, assuming exchangeable clean-option priors.
Extend DistractorRecall to 800 randomized items under 30% distractor-retaining paraphrase exposure; bootstrap power at a 5% clean-model FPR.
At 800 randomized items and 30% distractor-retaining exposure, DistractorRecall achieved 83% bootstrap power at 5% clean-model FPR.
Does DistractorRecall remain calibrated when clean models favor benchmark distractors because those options appeared independently in training?
Vary independent distractor exposure among clean models, stratify option-prior mismatch, and measure 800-item DistractorRecall FPR and power.
Stress-test 800-item DistractorRecall with 0–20% independent benchmark-distractor exposure in clean models; measure FPR and 30%-contamination power.
DistractorRecall exposure-sensitivity chart tabulates 800-item FPR and power across 0–20% independent clean-model distractor exposure.
Audit the DistractorRecall chart by exposure stratum; identify where 5% FPR or 80% power first fails.
At ≤2% independent distractor exposure, DistractorRecall retained 81% power and 4.9% FPR; at 10%, FPR rose to 9%.
Develop a partial-identification audit combining TwinTrace, TwinContrast, and DistractorRecall with negative controls to bound training-distribution mismatch.
Can negative-control prompts bound training-distribution mismatch tightly enough to certify 5% FPR without assuming controls share the target’s training distribution?
If negative controls bound clean target–control transcript-TV by 1%, a 4%-calibrated ensemble maintains ≤5% FPR without training-distribution equality.
Define negative-control-to-target transport assumptions, bound transcript-TV at 1%, calibrate the ensemble to 4% FPR, and test 30% contamination.
Using TwinContrast’s map, simulate 1%-TV negative-control transport; calibrate ensemble to 4% and measure clean-target FPR and 30%-contamination power.
Under 1%-TV transcript transport, the 4%-calibrated ensemble yielded 4.8% clean-target FPR and 82% power at 30% contamination.
Challenge the 1%-TV, 4%-calibrated ensemble with the chart’s 10% clean distractor exposure; estimate transcript-TV and target FPR.
At 10% clean distractor exposure, transcript-TV reached 3.2% and ensemble FPR 7.1%, triggering the audit’s transport warning.
Certify only with justified ≤1% transcript-TV transport and ≤2% independent distractor exposure; flag other regimes for further calibration.
Run conditional audit: 500 TwinContrast pairs, 800 DistractorRecall items; verify ≥80% power and ≤5% FPR within transport bounds, flag response-equivalence.
Conditional audit report documents 500-pair/800-item power and FPR, transport assumptions, distractor-exposure limits, and response-equivalence impossibility.
